questions.prompt: T-101 assigned 200,000 customers; 85,080 searched. You want the effect of the new ranking on the people it can reach. Which comparison do you report?
options: Treatment customers who searched against all control customers
Customers who searched in treatment against customers who searched in control
All treatment customers against all control customers, because it uses more data
Each searcher's orders before and after the first search
questions.explanation: The same trigger rule in both arms keeps randomisation intact inside the triggered group, and leaves out customers the ranking could not affect.
misconceptions: Treats the trigger as a property of treatment only: the two groups then differ in who they are, not only in the ranking
Assumes more data is always better: the untriggered customers add noise and no effect
Confuses exposure with assignment: the timing of the first search is not randomised, so before and after is not a controlled comparison

questions.prompt: A 50/50 test shows +3% orders with p = 0.002. Its sample ratio check gives p = 0.0004: the treatment arm has 1.2% fewer users than planned. What do you do?
options: Report the lift: the arms are large and the gap is only 1.2%
Reweight the treatment arm up to 50% and report the adjusted lift
Report no result, find where users are lost, fix it and rerun
Correct both p-values for multiple testing and report what survives
questions.explanation: A mismatch means assignment did not work as planned, so the arms are no longer comparable. No analysis of the outcome repairs that.
misconceptions: Thinks a mismatch only costs a little precision; the missing users can create the whole lift
Assumes reweighting can restore randomisation; it cannot recover who was lost or why
Treats the sample ratio check as one more metric to correct for multiplicity, not as a test of the experiment itself

questions.prompt: The AI ranking lifts orders by 3.9% (interval well above zero). Its p95 latency is 420 ms worse; the pre-registered limit was 300 ms. What does the spec say?
options: Not a launch as is: the latency guardrail fails, so the decision rule applies
Launch: a 3.9% lift is worth more than 120 ms
Raise the latency limit to 450 ms and launch
Report latency as a side note to the primary result
questions.explanation: Guardrails were written before the test so that a good primary cannot buy them off. The rule decides what follows: for T-101, iterate on latency.
misconceptions: Treats guardrails as weights to trade against the primary, which is what writing them in advance prevents
Moves the threshold after seeing the data, which turns the guardrail into decoration
Confuses a guardrail with a diagnostic: latency here is a limit, not an explanation

questions.prompt: A test needs 41,000 customers per arm to detect a 2% lift in orders with 80% power. The product manager now wants to detect 1%. Roughly how many per arm?
questions.explanation: The sample size grows with one over the effect squared: half the effect needs four times the customers.
misconceptions: Assumes sample size grows in proportion to precision, when it grows with its square
Applies the square root the wrong way round
Confuses halving the effect with halving the power

questions.prompt: Ruba receives the results of a 28-day test with a 4% lift on the primary metric, all guardrails green. Which check does she run before reading any of it?
options: Regression adjustment, to narrow the interval
A false discovery correction over the segments
The sample ratio check on the assignment counts
A power calculation for the observed effect
questions.explanation: If the split is not what was planned, no metric of the test can be trusted, so that check comes before every other.
misconceptions: Puts precision before validity: a narrower interval on a broken test is still broken
Treats many segments as the first risk, when a broken split would void every segment too
Confuses a planning tool with a check of a finished test

questions.prompt: Ruba wants to cap order value at the 99th percentile for T-101's revenue metric. Which data should set the cap?
options: Order values from both arms pooled, or from history before the test
Order values of the control arm only
Each arm's own 99th percentile
Whichever cap gives the smallest p-value
questions.explanation: A cap must be the same rule for both arms and fixed independently of the result; pooled or historical data does both.
misconceptions: Thinks the control arm is neutral, but a cap from one arm still treats the arms differently
Believes each arm deserves its own percentile, which makes the metric depend on the treatment
Chooses the cap after seeing the result, which lets the analyst pick a favourable estimate

questions.prompt: Ruba wants a stronger adjustment for T-101 and considers adding one more covariate to the regression. Which one is safe?
options: Number of searches during the test
Revenue during the test
Day of the first search in the test
Revenue in the 28 pre-period days
questions.explanation: A covariate measured before assignment cannot be changed by the treatment, so adjusting for it removes noise without removing effect.
misconceptions: Ignores that searches after assignment can be changed by the new ranking, so the covariate carries part of the effect
Treats an outcome of the test as a covariate, which removes the effect itself
Forgets that the trigger day depends on behaviour during the test, which the treatment may affect in other tests

questions.prompt: A test randomises customers and reports clicks per page view: 1.9 million views, 80,000 customers. Which standard error should the analysis use?
options: The binomial standard error over 1.9 million views
A delta-method standard error over the 80,000 customers
The standard error of the mean of each customer's click rate
A bootstrap that resamples page views
questions.explanation: The variance must be computed over the unit that was randomised; the delta method does that for a ratio of sums.
misconceptions: Counts page views as independent trials, ignoring that one customer's views move together
Averages each customer's own rate, which answers a different question and weights light users like heavy ones
Resamples the wrong unit and reproduces the naive error

questions.prompt: Sufrah plans a 2,000-customer pilot in two cities whose customers order at very different rates. Which design reduces the variance of the estimate most?
options: A simple 50/50 randomisation, analysed as a simple difference
Strata for every district, analysed per district
Randomisation within each city, analysed with the city strata
A separate test in each city, reported side by side
questions.explanation: When the strata explain much of the variance and the test is small, randomising within strata prevents imbalance and removes the between-strata noise.
misconceptions: Thinks a simple randomisation always balances, which is only true on average and fails most in small samples
Believes more strata are always better; tiny strata give noisy means and unstable variances
Confuses reporting results per city with estimating the overall effect more precisely

questions.prompt: Ruba must narrow the interval of revenue per triggered customer in T-101 and keep estimating exactly the effect on revenue. Which method does that?
options: Capping each order at the 99th percentile
Regression adjustment on revenue in the 28 pre-period days
Dropping the customers with the largest orders
Switching to revenue per order
questions.explanation: A pre-period covariate removes predictable noise; its term has mean zero in each arm, so the expected difference, and so the estimand, is unchanged.
misconceptions: Forgets that a cap changes what is estimated: capped revenue, not revenue
Removes customers, which changes the population and the estimand
Changes the metric to a ratio with its own estimand

questions.prompt: A 28-day test with an O'Brien-Fleming plan shows z = 2.4 on day 5. The boundary on day 5 is infinite. Yazeed wants to launch. What do you tell him?
options: The result is significant at 5%, so launch
We should not have looked at day 5 at all
Keep running: the evidence has not crossed the planned boundary
Switch to a Pocock plan, whose day-5 boundary is lower
questions.explanation: The boundary is what keeps the false-win rate at 5% over all looks; crossing 1.96 early is common under no effect.
misconceptions: Applies the fixed-test threshold to a sequential plan, which is exactly the peeking error
Thinks a sequential plan forbids looking, when it only forbids acting below the boundary
Moves the plan after seeing the data

questions.prompt: The Luqma team will check results on a public dashboard several times a day and may stop at any moment. The test has no fixed end date. Which design keeps the false-win rate at 5%?
options: A fixed test at alpha = 0.01
A group sequential test with daily looks
A Bonferroni correction over the expected number of looks
An always-valid test such as mSPRT
questions.explanation: Only an always-valid test keeps its error rate whatever the number and timing of looks and with no fixed end.
misconceptions: Assumes a stricter fixed threshold solves repeated looks, without knowing how many there will be
Needs looks and a maximum fixed in advance, which this team cannot promise
Corrects for a known number of tests, but the number of looks is unknown

questions.prompt: Four tests are planned, each randomised by customer. Which result is most likely biased by interference between customers?
options: A new wording on the checkout button
A delivery-fee discount that raises orders at peak hours
A dark mode for the app
AI-ranked search for one customer's results
questions.explanation: More treated orders at peak load the same couriers that serve control customers, slowing them: the control arm is changed by the treatment.
misconceptions: A change of wording on a screen affects only the customer who sees it
A personal setting changes nothing for other customers
Search ranking shown to one customer does not use a resource others share, unless supply is scarce

questions.prompt: Joud's switchback randomised 1,176 city-hour blocks; they contain about 83,000 orders. Ruba computes the standard error from the 83,000 orders as independent rows. What is wrong?
options: The block was randomised, so the standard error must be computed over blocks
The estimate is biased by interference
Nothing: more rows give a more precise estimate
The first hour after each switch must always be dropped
questions.explanation: Orders in one block share the rule and the same couriers; treating them as independent repeats Day 2's ratio-metric mistake at a larger scale.
misconceptions: Thinks the problem is the estimate, not its variance; the mean difference can be fine
Confuses a power shortfall with a variance error; more orders do not make them independent
Assumes carryover is the main error, when it is the unit of analysis

questions.prompt: Joud wants the effect of giving priority to orders under a new dispatch rule, as it would be if every order in a city used it. Customer randomisation showed a 10.4-minute gain. Which design answers her question?
options: Customer randomisation with twice the traffic
Order randomisation within each customer
A city-by-hour switchback, analysed over blocks
Customer randomisation with a Bonferroni correction
questions.explanation: In a block every order runs the same rule, so the couriers are not shared between arms and the difference between blocks estimates the global effect.
misconceptions: Keeps the shared couriers that caused the transfer of waiting between arms
Moves the unit to the order, which shares couriers even more tightly
Corrects for many metrics, not for interference between units

questions.prompt: A new AI menu search raises allergen complaints by +0.10 per 1,000 orders, 95% interval -0.20 to +0.40. The pre-registered limit is +0.30 on the upper bound. What does the rule say?
options: It holds: the difference is not significantly above zero
It fails: the upper bound, +0.40, is above the limit
It holds: the estimate, +0.10, is below the limit
It cannot be judged without a longer test
questions.explanation: The test must show the harm is below the limit. An interval that reaches +0.40 has not shown that; a larger test might.
misconceptions: Reads a difference that is not significant as evidence of no harm
Judges harm on the estimate, which lets a noisy test pass
Thinks a test can never judge harm, when the upper bound does exactly that

questions.prompt: Ruba cut a test into 20 city-and-platform segments. One, Abha on Android, has p = 0.01; the other nineteen are above 0.2. With Benjamini-Hochberg at 5%, what does she report?
options: A win in Abha on Android, because 0.01 is below 0.05
A win with a 1% chance of being false
That segment analysis is never allowed
No segment survives: 0.01 is above its threshold, 0.05 × 1 / 20 = 0.0025
questions.explanation: Benjamini-Hochberg compares the k-th smallest p-value with 0.05 × k / 20. The smallest, 0.01, is above 0.0025, and no larger p-value meets its own threshold (the last one is 0.05), so nothing is reported.
misconceptions: Applies the single-test threshold to one test chosen from twenty
Thinks the false discovery rate is the same as the p-value of the best segment
Confuses the smallest-p threshold with a ban on segments

questions.prompt: Rawan's board reads one page per test. Ruba's draft for T-101 opens with the method, then the data, then the effect, and ends with the decision. What should she change?
options: Put the decision and its reason first; the evidence follows
Put the guardrail table first, because it decided
Drop the interval and keep the point estimate
Add a methods appendix to the page
questions.explanation: The reader decides; the page leads with the decision so every number after it can be checked against it.
misconceptions: Moves detail up when the reader needs the conclusion first
Hides the uncertainty the board needs to judge the decision
Adds length when the problem is the order

questions.prompt: A write-up reports +3.0% over four weeks, interval 1.6% to 4.4%, and recommends launch. Its weekly lifts are 7.1%, 2.8%, 0.9% and 0.2%, each with a standard error of 0.8 points. What does the board decide?
options: Launch: the four-week interval is above zero
Stop: the result is novelty, so there is no effect
Iterate: run longer, because the settled effect is not shown to be above zero
Apply Benjamini-Hochberg to the four weeks
questions.explanation: Week 4's interval, 0.2% ± 1.6 points, includes zero; the board needs the settled effect before a launch.
misconceptions: Takes the four-week average as the settled effect when the weekly lifts show it fading
Stops for a fault that is not harm; the idea may still have a small settled effect
Applies a segment correction to a question about time

questions.prompt: A test of a new filter on the restaurant list assigns 120,000 customers; 30,000 open the filter panel, which is logged in both arms. Which population gives the most precise unbiased estimate of the filter's effect?
options: Everyone assigned, because the sample is four times larger
Customers who opened the panel, in both arms
Treatment customers who opened the panel against all control customers
Customers who used the filter at least once, in treatment only
questions.explanation: The same trigger rule in both arms keeps the randomised comparison and leaves out customers the change could not reach.
misconceptions: Thinks more rows always mean more precision; the 90,000 who never open the panel add noise and no effect
Cuts only one arm, so the comparison is between different kinds of customers
Conditions on a behaviour the treatment causes and drops the control group

questions.prompt: A test triggers 25% of assigned customers and shows a 6% lift among them, with similar baselines in both groups. Roughly what lift should the analysis over everyone assigned show?
options: Nothing can be said without rerunning the test
6%, because the effect is a property of the change
24%, the triggered lift divided by the trigger rate
questions.explanation: The overall effect is the triggered effect times the share triggered: 6% x 0.25 = 1.5%.
misconceptions: Does not see that dilution is arithmetic when baselines are similar
Forgets that untriggered customers contribute zero effect to the average
Applies the dilution in the wrong direction

questions.prompt: A 50/50 test shows a 2.5% lift with p = 0.01. Its sample ratio check gives p = 0.0002; the treatment arm is short of users on one browser. What should the analyst report?
options: The lift, after reweighting the arms to 50/50
The lift, with a note on the mismatch
The lift computed on the other browsers only
No result until the cause is fixed and the test rerun
questions.explanation: A sample ratio mismatch means assignment did not work as planned, so the outcome comparison cannot be trusted.
misconceptions: Believes weights can restore what randomisation lost
Treats a broken split as a minor caveat, when the missing users can create the lift
Assumes the loss is confined to one browser and that the rest stays randomised, which nobody has shown

questions.prompt: Five hundred A/A reshuffles of last month's data, analysed with the team's standard test, give 11% of p-values below 0.05. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A/A tests always show more false wins than 5%
Last month had unusual traffic
The analysis is miscalibrated, for example tested at a smaller unit than the one randomised
Five hundred reshuffles are too few to say anything
questions.explanation: A correct analysis gives about 5% false wins on A/A splits; a much higher rate means its variance is underestimated, often because the unit of analysis is wrong.
misconceptions: Thinks false-win inflation is a property of A/A tests rather than of the analysis
Confuses the data with the procedure: reshuffles of any month should give about 5%
Overlooks that 11% is far outside the 5% band for 500 reshuffles (about plus or minus 2 points)

questions.prompt: A pre-registered test of an AI search ranking has orders per customer as primary and a latency guardrail of at most +300 ms at p95. Results: orders +3% (interval above zero), p95 latency +410 ms. What follows?
options: Launch, and raise the latency limit for the next test
Not a launch as is: apply the written decision rule for a failed guardrail
Rerun the test with latency as the primary metric
Launch, since the primary metric won
questions.explanation: A guardrail is a limit written before the test; when it fails, the pre-registered rule decides, whatever the primary shows.
misconceptions: Moves a threshold after seeing the data
Confuses a guardrail with a goal
Treats guardrails as advisory, which defeats writing them in advance

questions.prompt: A harm guardrail says complaints per 1,000 orders must not rise by more than 1.0. The estimate is +0.3 with a 95% interval from -0.5 to +1.4. Does the guardrail hold?
options: No, because the upper bound exceeds 1.0
No, because any rise in complaints fails a harm guardrail
Yes, because the estimate is below 1.0
Yes, because the difference is not statistically significant
questions.explanation: A harm guardrail holds only when the interval rules out a rise beyond the margin; an upper bound of 1.4 does not.
misconceptions: Ignores the margin the guardrail states
Reads the point estimate where a non-inferiority guardrail needs the interval
Treats "no evidence of harm" as evidence of no harm

questions.prompt: A test analysis needs the number of complaints per order. The data team offers the complaint category and the full complaint text, both collected for customer support and product improvement. Which should the analysis use?
options: Neither, because complaints are personal data
Both, because more detail gives a better metric
The text only, because categories can be wrong
The category only
questions.explanation: The category carries what the metric needs; reading the free text would exceed the minimum necessary for the purpose.
misconceptions: Thinks personal data can never be used, when the law allows use for the purpose collected and within the minimum necessary
Ignores that the content must be limited to what the purpose needs
Picks the more identifying field for a count the category already gives

questions.prompt: A test needs 30,000 customers per arm to detect a 3% lift with 80% power. How many per arm are needed to detect a 1.5% lift with the same power?
questions.explanation: Sample size grows with one over the effect squared: half the effect needs four times the customers.
misconceptions: Scales the sample size linearly with precision
Scales by the square root of two
Thinks a smaller effect needs fewer customers

questions.prompt: Why size a test by simulation on historical data when a formula exists?
options: The formula is only valid for proportions
Simulation uses the metric's real distribution and the exact analysis that will be run
Simulation always gives a smaller sample size
The formula needs the effect size, which simulation does not
questions.explanation: Simulation keeps the real tail and any analysis choice (triggering, capping, sequential looks) that a closed formula may not describe.
misconceptions: Thinks the two-sample formula does not cover means
Expects simulation to be more optimistic, when it can go either way
Overlooks that a simulation also needs the effect it injects

questions.prompt: An analyst caps basket value for a promotion test at each arm's own 99th percentile. The treatment arm has more large baskets. What is the problem?
options: The cap now depends on the treatment, so it can create or hide a difference
A 99th percentile cap is too loose to matter
None: each arm is treated by the same rule
The treatment arm is capped lower in relative terms than control
questions.explanation: A cap must be one value for both arms, fixed from pooled or historical data; per-arm caps make the metric depend on the treatment.
misconceptions: Ignores that the issue is where the cap comes from, not how tight it is
Thinks "the same percentile" means the same rule, when the cap values then differ by arm
Gets the direction of the distortion wrong

questions.prompt: Capping order value at a lower percentile always reduces the standard error of revenue per customer. Why not cap at the median?
options: A median cap would make the sample ratio check fail
Regulators forbid capping below the 90th percentile
The standard error would rise again below some cap
The estimand moves away from revenue and the bias grows until it dominates the error
questions.explanation: Each tighter cap removes noise but shifts what is estimated; past some point the bias costs more than the noise saved.
misconceptions: Confuses a metric transformation with assignment
Invents a rule; the limit is statistical, not regulatory
Thinks the variance curve turns back up, when it keeps falling

questions.prompt: The correlation between a metric in the pre-period and in the test period is 0.6. Regression adjustment on the pre-period gives roughly what effective sample-size gain?
options: 1.6 times
2.5 times
1.56 times
No gain, because the pre-period has no treatment effect
questions.explanation: The variance falls by a factor 1 - 0.36 = 0.64, so the gain is 1 / 0.64, about 1.56 times the customers.
misconceptions: Adds the correlation to one instead of using its square
Uses one over (1 - rho) instead of one over (1 - rho squared)
Confuses carrying no effect with carrying no information about the noise

questions.prompt: Which covariate can safely be used for regression adjustment in a test of a new checkout page?
options: Number of checkout page views during the test
Orders in the 28 days before assignment
Whether the customer saw the new page
Orders in the test period
questions.explanation: A covariate measured before assignment cannot be affected by the treatment, so it removes noise without removing effect.
misconceptions: Uses a variable the treatment can change, which absorbs part of the effect
Conditions on exposure, which differs by arm by design
Adjusts the outcome for itself and removes the effect

questions.prompt: Why is the CUPED coefficient theta estimated on both arms pooled rather than separately in each arm?
options: Separate slopes can absorb part of the treatment effect into the adjustment
Pooling makes the pre-period means equal
The control arm's slope would always be zero
It is faster to compute once
questions.explanation: With one pooled theta the adjustment depends only on habits; arm-specific slopes let the adjustment differ by arm and bias the difference.
misconceptions: Randomisation, not pooling, makes the pre-period means equal in expectation
Misunderstands the slope as an effect of the treatment
Gives a convenience reason for a validity question

questions.prompt: A test randomises customers and reports revenue per order. The analyst computes the standard error as the standard deviation of order values over the square root of the number of orders. What happens?
options: The estimate is biased but the interval is right
The interval is about right, because orders are many
The interval is too wide
The interval is too narrow, because one customer's orders are correlated
questions.explanation: Orders of one customer move together; treating them as independent understates the variance. The delta method over customers fixes it.
misconceptions: Locates the error in the point estimate instead of its variance
Thinks a large count makes rows independent
Gets the direction wrong: ignoring positive within-customer correlation makes intervals too narrow

questions.prompt: To check a delta-method interval for orders per session in a customer-randomised test, what should a bootstrap resample?
options: Days, because traffic varies by day
Orders, because they are the numerator
Customers, each with all their sessions and orders
Sessions, because the metric is per session
questions.explanation: The bootstrap must copy how the data was produced: customers were drawn and randomised, so customers are resampled.
misconceptions: Picks a unit that was neither sampled nor randomised
Breaks the link between numerator and denominator
Resamples the unit of analysis, reproducing the naive error

questions.prompt: In which design is a session-level binomial interval for orders per session correct?
options: When every customer has at least ten sessions
When each session is randomised on its own and sessions are independent
When the test is large
Never: ratio metrics always need a bootstrap
questions.explanation: The binomial interval assumes independent trials; that holds when sessions are the randomised, independent unit.
misconceptions: Thinks more sessions per customer make them independent
Confuses sample size with the independence assumption
Overlooks that the naive interval is right when the unit of analysis is the randomisation unit

questions.prompt: Post-stratifying a 90,000-customer test by city barely changes its standard error. What is the most likely reason?
options: The cities explain little of the variance of the metric
Post-stratification only works with stratified assignment
The weights should be the treatment arm's city shares
The test is too small for strata to help
questions.explanation: Strata remove only the variance between strata; when cities explain about 1% of it, little is gained.
misconceptions: Thinks post-stratification needs design-stage strata
Changes the estimand without touching the variance
Has the size effect backwards: imbalance, and so the gain, is larger in small tests

questions.prompt: In a post-stratified estimate, each city's difference in means is weighted by what?
options: The city's share of the treatment arm
The inverse of the city's variance, to favour precise cities
Equal weights, one per city
The city's share of all customers in the test
questions.explanation: Weighting by each city's share of all customers keeps the estimand the average effect over the test population.
misconceptions: Uses one arm's mix, which chance imbalance can distort
Describes a precision-weighted estimate, which targets a different average
Gives a small city the same say as a large one, changing the estimand

questions.prompt: A team checks a test with no true effect every day for four weeks and stops the first time p < 0.05. Roughly what false-win rate should they expect?
options: Under 5%, because later looks have more data
5%, because each look uses alpha = 0.05
Between 20% and 30%
76%, which is 1 - 0.95 to the power 28
questions.explanation: Daily looks at accumulating data are correlated, so the rate is far below the independent-tests figure but far above 5%; the course simulator gives 28%.
misconceptions: Thinks more data per look lowers the chance of crossing at some look
Treats each look as if it were the only one
Treats correlated daily looks as independent tests

questions.prompt: Why does an O'Brien-Fleming boundary start very high and end near 2?
options: Because early data is more likely to contain errors
Because it spends almost no alpha early and nearly all of it at the planned end
Because the effect grows over time
Because the variance grows with each look
questions.explanation: The spending function allots tiny alpha to early looks, so early boundaries are strict and the last look keeps close to the full 5%.
misconceptions: Confuses data quality with the statistical design
Thinks the boundary tracks the effect rather than the error rate
Gets the direction wrong: the standard error shrinks as data accrues

questions.prompt: A test with a group sequential plan shows z = 2.3 on day 6; the day-6 boundary is 3.6. The product owner asks to launch now. What is the right answer?
options: Keep running: the evidence has not crossed the planned boundary
Stop for futility: the effect is too small
Restart the test with a lower boundary
Launch: 2.3 is above 1.96
questions.explanation: Acting below the planned boundary would bring back the false-win inflation the plan prevents.
misconceptions: Confuses not crossing the efficacy boundary with evidence of no effect
Changes the plan after seeing data
Applies the fixed-horizon threshold to a sequential plan

questions.prompt: What property lets an mSPRT keep its false-positive rate at or below alpha however often it is checked?
options: It only allows looks once a day
It uses a smaller alpha than a fixed test
Its threshold rises with every look
Under no effect its likelihood ratio is a martingale with mean 1, so it rarely reaches 1 / alpha
questions.explanation: By Ville's inequality, the chance that a mean-one nonnegative martingale ever reaches 1 / alpha is at most alpha.
misconceptions: Thinks the guarantee depends on a fixed look schedule
Confuses the mechanism with a stricter threshold
Describes a correction schedule the mSPRT does not need

questions.prompt: A test has a fixed 28-day maximum, daily batches of data and a team that will act only at planned looks. Which sequential design gives the most power while controlling false wins?
options: Daily checks at alpha = 0.05 with a two-day confirmation rule
An always-valid test, because it is valid at any time
A group sequential design with alpha spending
A fixed test with a Bonferroni correction for 28 looks
questions.explanation: When the maximum and the looks are known in advance, a group sequential design spends alpha for exactly that plan and has the most power.
misconceptions: Invents an informal rule with an unknown error rate
Pays for flexibility that is not needed here
Overcorrects by ignoring the correlation between looks

questions.prompt: In an mSPRT, what does a much larger mixture width tau do?
options: It raises the false-positive rate above alpha
It tunes the test to larger effects: quicker on big ones, weaker on small ones
It makes the test equivalent to a fixed test
It has no effect once the sample is large
questions.explanation: tau sets which effects the mixture weights most; the error guarantee holds for any tau.
misconceptions: Thinks tau trades away validity; it only trades power between effect sizes
Confuses tuning with the design family
Overlooks that tau shapes the statistic at every sample size

questions.prompt: A food-delivery test gives treated customers priority for the next free courier, randomised by customer. The treated arm shows 10 minutes faster delivery. What is the best reading?
options: The difference mostly measures waiting moved from control to treated orders
The test is invalid because of a sample ratio mismatch
The rule saves about 10 minutes and should launch
The rule saves about 5 minutes, half of the difference
questions.explanation: Shared couriers break no-interference: the difference counts the transfer of waiting twice, and says little about the effect of running the rule for everyone.
misconceptions: Names a different fault; nothing here suggests the split broke
Ignores that control customers lost the minutes the treated gained
Guesses a fixed share instead of measuring the global effect

questions.prompt: Which test is most exposed to interference between customers?
options: A larger font on the menu page
A new order-tracking animation
A new icon for the favourites list
A courier bonus that changes which orders couriers accept
questions.explanation: Couriers serve both arms; changing their behaviour for treated orders changes service for control orders.
misconceptions: A personal display change affects nobody else
Changes what one customer sees, not a shared resource
A purely visual change affects only the viewer

questions.prompt: A switchback randomised 1,200 city-hour blocks. How should the standard error of the effect be computed?
options: It cannot be computed; switchbacks need a Bayesian analysis
Over the orders in all blocks, as independent rows
Over the blocks, the unit that was randomised
Over the six cities only
questions.explanation: The unit of analysis matches the unit of randomisation: the block.
misconceptions: Thinks the design rules out a frequentist interval
Treats orders as the randomised unit, which understates the variance
Uses a coarser unit than the one randomised and wastes the design

questions.prompt: What does a city-by-hour switchback give up in exchange for removing interference between customers?
options: Nothing: it is better in every way
Power, because there are far fewer randomised units and they vary a lot
Validity, because cities differ
The ability to measure delivery time
questions.explanation: A switchback has hundreds or thousands of blocks in place of hundreds of thousands of customers, so it needs more time for the same power.
misconceptions: Overlooks the loss of power from far fewer, noisier units
Fixed effects and randomisation within city handle city differences
Confuses the design with what can be measured

questions.prompt: How can an analyst check whether carryover between hours biases a switchback before running it?
options: Simulate the design with and without carryover and compare the estimates
Use one-hour blocks, which have no carryover
Weight blocks by orders
Run an A/A switchback in production for a month
questions.explanation: Simulating the design with the nuisance switched on and off measures its bias directly.
misconceptions: Gets it backwards: short blocks are where carryover matters most
Confuses the weighting question with the carryover question
Uses an expensive check that cannot see carryover of a real effect

questions.prompt: An AI assistant test shows allergen complaints up by 0.1 per 1,000 orders, 95% interval -0.2 to +0.5. The pre-registered harm limit is +0.3 on the upper bound. What does the rule say?
options: The harm guardrail holds, because the estimate is below the limit
The guardrail cannot be judged until the test ends
The harm guardrail holds, because the difference is not significant
The harm guardrail fails, because the upper bound is above the limit
questions.explanation: The test must show the harm is below the limit; an upper bound of +0.5 has not shown that.
misconceptions: Judges harm on the estimate, which lets a noisy test pass
Thinks the rule needs more than the interval it was written for
Reads absence of evidence of harm as evidence of safety

questions.prompt: Which pair of guardrails does an AI chat feature need that a new button usually does not?
options: Revenue per order and basket size
Click-through rate and page views
Response time in the tail and cost per conversation
Sample ratio and trigger rate
questions.explanation: A model call is slow and paid for, so its tail latency and its cost each need a pre-registered limit.
misconceptions: Names business metrics, not the costs a model adds
Names engagement metrics that apply to any feature
Names trustworthiness checks every test needs

questions.prompt: A test's weekly lifts are 5.8%, 2.5%, 0.5% and -0.5%; the four-week average is +2.1%. What should the write-up report as the long-run effect?
options: +5.8%, the first week, because that is when customers noticed
The weekly pattern, with the last weeks as the settled effect, which is not shown to be above zero
Nothing: novelty makes the test invalid
+2.1%, the four-week average, because it uses all the data
questions.explanation: When the lift fades, the last weeks estimate the settled effect; the average overstates it.
misconceptions: Reports the novelty peak as the effect
Thinks a fading effect breaks the test rather than changing what it shows
Averages a novelty spike into the long-run estimate

questions.prompt: Sufrah's loyalty team launched three features in a half-year, each after a 14-day test: +1.6%, +1.1% and +1.1% in orders per customer. A 10% holdout kept on the old app reads, launched over holdout: +0.9%, +0.9%, +1.1%, +0.4% (interval -0.5% to +1.2%), +1.0%, and +1.1% (interval 0.2% to 2.0%) in month six. What should the team report as the long-run effect of the three launches?
options: +3.8%, the sum of the three 14-day test wins, each of them significant
No lasting effect: the month-four interval includes zero
+1.1%, the holdout's month-six reading, interval 0.2% to 2.0%
+1.3%, the mean of the three test wins
questions.explanation: Short tests include novelty and do not add up; the holdout measures the combined, settled effect, and its later months agree with each other.
misconceptions: Adds short-test wins as if each lasts and none overlaps
Judges a steady series by its one noisy month
Averages per-feature test lifts instead of measuring the combined launch

questions.prompt: A test is cut into 20 independent segments with no true effect in any. About how often does at least one segment show p below 0.05?
options: About 64% of the time
Every time
About 25% of the time
5% of the time
questions.explanation: The chance of no false win is 0.95 to the power 20, about 0.36, so at least one appears about 64% of the time.
misconceptions: Confuses the expected one false win with a certain one
Guesses without the 1 - 0.95^20 calculation
Treats twenty tests as one

questions.prompt: An analyst explores 20 segments to find leads for follow-up tests and can accept that a few of the leads are false. Which correction fits?
options: Holm, because it controls the false discovery rate
Bonferroni, because it is the strictest
None, because the segments are only exploratory
Benjamini-Hochberg, which controls the share of false leads among those reported
questions.explanation: The false discovery rate is the right target for a list of leads; the family-wise rate suits a single costly claim.
misconceptions: Confuses the family-wise error rate with the false discovery rate
Picks the strictest control when a share of false leads is acceptable
Forgets that uncorrected exploration produces false leads at a known high rate

questions.prompt: A segment survives Benjamini-Hochberg in a test whose overall result was flat. What should happen next?
options: Discard it, because segment analysis is never valid
Launch the change for that segment only
Run a new test pre-registered on that segment
Report the overall result as a win
questions.explanation: A corrected survivor is a lead worth confirming; a new pre-registered test confirms it.
misconceptions: Treats a corrected finding as worthless instead of as a lead
Acts on a post-hoc finding without confirming it
Lets a segment change the reading of the overall result

questions.prompt: T-101's primary interval is well above zero; the latency guardrail fails; the harm guardrail holds. The pre-registered rule says stop on harm, launch if all guardrails hold, otherwise iterate. What is the decision?
options: Stop, because a guardrail failed
Iterate, because a non-harm guardrail failed
Extend the test until latency improves
Launch, because the lift is large
questions.explanation: Applied literally, the rule gives iterate: fix latency, then confirm.
misconceptions: Treats a non-harm guardrail as harm
Changes the test instead of applying the rule
Overrides the written rule after seeing the result

questions.prompt: What comes first on a one-page recommendation to a review board?
options: The decision and its reason
The full table of all metrics
The risks
The method and the data sources
questions.explanation: The reader decides; the page opens with the decision so each number after it can be checked against it.
misconceptions: Leads with detail instead of the conclusion
Puts the caveats before the claim they qualify
Puts what the reader checks later before what the reader decides

questions.prompt: A write-up reports a clean 2.1% lift. Its users are 50,912 treatment and 49,088 control on a planned 50/50 split. What does the board decide?
options: Stop: the feature caused customers to leave
Launch at half traffic
Launch: the interval is above zero
Iterate: the sample ratio mismatch makes the result untrustworthy until its cause is fixed
questions.explanation: A chi-square p-value of about 10^-8 says the arms differ in who is in them; every later number is suspect.
misconceptions: Assumes a cause for the mismatch without evidence
Picks a compromise the rule does not contain
Reads the result before checking the split

questions.prompt: A write-up stopped on day 9 when the daily p-value first fell below 0.05. The pre-registered plan had a day-9 boundary of z = 3.47, and the planned day-28 analysis gives z = 0.27. What does the board decide?
options: Launch, because p was below 0.05
Iterate, to run the test again
Stop: the planned analysis shows no effect
Launch, because day 9 was early evidence
questions.explanation: No day crossed the planned boundary, and the day-28 analysis the plan called for found nothing.
misconceptions: Applies the fixed-test threshold to a peek
Iterates on an idea the planned analysis found no effect for
Treats an early crossing of 1.96 as stronger evidence, when it is weaker

questions.prompt: A courier batching change cut delivery cost by 6%; courier earnings per online hour fell by 4.2% (interval -5.9% to -2.5%) against a pre-registered limit of -2%. The team recommends launch for the saving. What does the board decide?
options: Iterate: lower the earnings limit to -5%
Stop: the harm guardrail fails
Launch in one city first
Launch: the saving is large
questions.explanation: The whole interval is below the limit; the board stops a test whose harm guardrail worsens.
misconceptions: Moves a pre-registered limit after seeing the data
Picks a compromise that still ships a change whose harm guardrail failed
Lets the primary metric override a harm guardrail
